context: Flask checkout API · mobile clients retry on timeout · Stripe-style payments API
title: Pay-for-order endpoint

reasons.text: A client or gateway retry after a timeout runs the charge again, because nothing ties the request to a single charge.
Reading total_cents at request time lets the price change between the lookup and the charge, billing the wrong amount.
The currency is hardcoded to usd, so customers billed in other currencies are charged the wrong amount in production.
Returning the charge id to the client exposes an internal payment identifier that attackers can use to guess other charges.

productionImpact: On a flaky mobile network the first request succeeds at the provider but the response is lost. The app retries, and the customer is charged twice. Any money-moving endpoint must accept an idempotency key and return the original result on replay.
interviewNote: Interview angle: 'what if the network drops after the server did the work?' is the idempotency question.

context: Flask + SQLAlchemy · 4 gunicorn workers · single-use coupons · 200 req/s at peak
title: Coupon redemption
code:
def redeem(code: str, user_id: int) -> bool:
    coupon = Coupon.query.filter_by(code=code).one()
    if coupon.redeemed_at is not None:
        return False
    coupon.redeemed_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    coupon.redeemed_by = user_id
    db.session.add(Redemption(coupon_id=coupon.id, user_id=user_id))
    db.session.commit()
    return True

reasons.text: Two concurrent requests can both see the coupon unredeemed before either commits, so a single-use coupon is redeemed twice.
Storing the timestamp in UTC rather than local time makes the redemption window shift by an hour during DST changes.
Using .one() raises when the code is unknown, so mistyped codes return a 500 instead of a clean validation message.
Adding the Redemption row in the same session as the update means a failure there silently drops the coupon change.

productionImpact: The check and the write are separate steps with a gap between them. With four workers at 200 req/s, a double-click or a retry lands two requests inside that gap, and both succeed. It passes every sequential test.
interviewNote: Fix with one atomic conditional UPDATE and check the affected-row count, not SELECT-then-UPDATE.

context: Export endpoint · 50k order ids per call · Postgres over the network, 2 ms round trip
title: Order export

reasons.text: One query per order id means 50k round trips per export, so latency and database load grow linearly with the batch size.
Collecting results into a list holds all 50k orders in memory at once, which will exhaust the worker's heap.
Passing oid as a bound parameter stops Postgres reusing a cached plan, so each lookup is planned from scratch.
Selecting named columns instead of star blocks index-only scans on order_lines, so each query reads the full heap.

productionImpact: 50,000 queries × 2 ms of network time is 100 seconds before any work happens, and it hammers the connection pool. It's fast on a dev laptop with 20 ids and a local database; it only shows up at production batch sizes.
interviewNote: Queries inside loops are the N+1 smell — look for I/O in a for.

context: Checkout · 20 gunicorn sync workers · carrier API hangs a few times a month
title: Shipping quote lookup

reasons.text: With no timeout, a hung carrier API blocks each worker forever, so all 20 workers stick and checkout goes down.
requests.post opens a new TCP connection on every call, which exhausts ephemeral ports under sustained checkout traffic.
raise_for_status turns every 4xx from the carrier into an exception, so one bad zip code takes the whole checkout down.
The quote price is trusted blindly, so a carrier response with a negative number would give customers free shipping.

productionImpact: requests has no default timeout: a connection that never answers waits forever. Each hung call pins one of 20 workers; after 20 stuck requests the whole site returns 502s although the CPU is idle and every dashboard looks healthy.
interviewNote: Every outbound call needs a timeout. 'No timeout' is a default in many libraries, not a safe choice.

context: Express + Postgres · product catalog · pages are 1-based in the public API docs
title: Catalog pagination

reasons.text: Pages are 1-based but the offset is not shifted, so the first 20 products are never returned and every page is off by one.
OFFSET pagination re-scans the skipped rows, so deep pages get slower and eventually time out on a large table.
The page size is fixed at 20, so clients on large screens must issue many requests to render a single list.
ORDER BY id with no secondary key makes the sort unstable, so rows can repeat across pages when ids tie.

productionImpact: Page 1 starts at offset 20, so the 20 newest or lowest-id products are unreachable through the API, and the last page request asks past the end. Nobody notices because every page 'looks' full.
interviewNote: Write the off-by-one test: request page 1 and assert the first row.

context: Homepage 2k req/s · compute_stats runs ~8 s of heavy SQL · Redis cache with 60 s TTL
title: Homepage stats cache

reasons.text: When the key expires, every concurrent request misses and runs the 8 second query at once, overwhelming the database.
A 60 second TTL means visitors see stale numbers, so the homepage statistics will often be a minute out of date.
Storing JSON strings instead of native objects costs CPU on every cache hit and slows the hot path measurably.
cache.get returning None for an empty result makes the stats get recomputed on every single request.

productionImpact: For 59 seconds all is well. The moment the key expires, thousands of requests per second see a miss and each launches the 8 second query. The database falls over, so nobody repopulates the cache, and the outage feeds itself.
interviewNote: Mitigations: single-flight lock, stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs, background refresh.

context: Spring Boot service · Tomcat with 200 threads · timestamps formatted in order exports
title: Shared date formatter

reasons.text: SimpleDateFormat has mutable internal state, so a shared static instance garbles or throws under concurrent calls.
HH is the 24-hour field, so afternoon times are formatted as morning times in the exported file.
The pattern string is compiled again on each class load, which slows application startup noticeably.
parse declares ParseException, which forces callers into broad catch blocks that hide real failures.

productionImpact: SimpleDateFormat uses an internal Calendar while formatting. Under concurrent calls threads overwrite each other's fields, producing wrong dates or NumberFormatException — only under load, never in a single-threaded test.
interviewNote: Classic Java trap. java.time formatters are immutable and thread-safe; SimpleDateFormat is not.

context: Spring Boot · HikariCP pool of 10 connections · some lookups hit missing account ids
title: Balance lookup

reasons.text: If the query throws or no row exists, execution skips close(), so connections leak until the pool is exhausted and requests hang.
Closing the connection before the ResultSet and statement are closed discards the pending results and can return a wrong balance.
Preparing the statement on every call defeats statement caching and makes each lookup slower than a plain Statement would.
The lookup runs outside any transaction, so another thread can change the balance between the query and the return.

productionImpact: A lookup for a missing id throws from getLong, skipping close(). Each such request permanently removes one of the 10 pooled connections; after ten of them every request blocks waiting for a connection and the whole service appears hung.

context: Flask · payment provider webhooks · provider retries any non-2xx for 3 days
title: Payment webhook

reasons.text: A 200 is returned even when processing failed, so the provider never retries and the paid order stays unpaid for good.
Catching Exception also catches KeyboardInterrupt, so a shutdown signal during processing is swallowed and the worker hangs.
Logging at warning level instead of error means the failures never reach the on-call alerting pipeline.
Returning 204 for other event types makes the provider assume the event was dropped and resend it repeatedly.

productionImpact: The provider's retry mechanism is your safety net, and a blanket 200 disables it. A transient database error leaves a customer who paid, with an order that still says unpaid and nobody alerted, until support tickets arrive.
interviewNote: Return success only after the work succeeded. Make the handler idempotent so retries are safe.

context: Merchant dashboard · API servers run in UTC · merchants in 40 countries · shows 'today's sales'
title: Today's sales total

reasons.text: Midnight is computed in the server's timezone, not the merchant's, so 'today' is wrong for most merchants and shifts at odd hours.
A SUM over a large orders table without a covering index scans every order for the merchant on each dashboard load.
Date objects are mutable, so setHours changes the shared start value that other requests are also reading at the time.
The nullish fallback hides the difference between zero sales and a missing value, so errors show up as empty days.

productionImpact: A merchant in Sydney sees yesterday's late sales as 'today' until 10am, and a merchant in Los Angeles sees 'today' reset at 4pm. The numbers are internally consistent, so it looks plausible, and finance catches it weeks later.
interviewNote: Store UTC, compute day boundaries in the user's zone. Never use server-local time for business days.
